claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoparticles are AuCoCuNiPt high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with a nearly equiatomic composition.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous atomic distribution.
In situ high-resolution TEM equipped with a heating stage can reveal atomic-scale structural changes during heating.
Observed lattice distortions and atomic rearrangements can demonstrate thermodynamic stabilization of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at high temperature.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles possess enhanced high-temperature structural stability.
A controlled thermal ramp will be performed in an HR-TEM using a precise heating stage.
The experiment will be conducted under high vacuum from room temperature to above the expected onset of structural transformations or atomic rearrangements.
Heating can produce defects or phase domains in the nanoparticle atomic lattice.
Thermal energy induces lattice distortions in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermal energy may induce phase transitions and atomic diffusion in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Heating-induced structural changes can relieve internal stresses or produce atomic ordering.
Stress relief, phase changes, diffusion, or ordering modify the free-energy landscape and thereby contribute to enhanced thermal stability.
Real-time HR-TEM imaging during heating will reveal changes in lattice spacing.
Real-time HR-TEM imaging during heating will reveal defect formation or reorientation.
Real-time HR-TEM imaging during heating will reveal the emergence of ordered domains.
Room-temperature images will show a uniform, defect-minimized lattice.
Atomic-scale TEM observations require sufficiently electron-transparent nanoparticles and are limited by the thermal and spatial resolution of the heating stage.
Electron-beam effects and sample-preparation artifacts can complicate attribution of observed structural changes to heating.
A room-temperature control can be compared with incrementally heated nanoparticles to assess heating-induced structural evolution.
Failure to detect significant atomic-scale changes during heating would falsify the proposed atomic-rearrangement mechanism for enhanced thermal stability.
